title: Electrons that jump
question: What happens inside an atom when it absorbs energy?
hook: An atom never glides smoothly between energies; its electrons leap, and each leap pays out an exact photon.
idea: Electrons sit in bound states, and absorbing or releasing energy moves them between states or frees them entirely.

beats.prompt: An electron in an atom absorbs a little less energy than its binding energy. What happens?

choices.label: It moves to an excited state
It is ejected with leftover energy
choices.feedback: Ejection needs more than the binding energy; this electron fell short.

choices.label: It absorbs nothing at all
choices.feedback: The electron does take the energy up, just not enough to escape.

beats.explain: With less than the binding energy the electron goes to an excited state; only more than that ionizes the atom.

beats.prompt: Put these in order for an atom that gets excited and then relaxes.
items: Electron sits in its ground state
Electron absorbs energy from a photon or collision
Electron jumps up to an excited state
Electron drops down and the atom emits a photon
beats.explain: Absorbed energy lifts an electron, and when it jumps down the atom emits a photon with the energy difference.
Atomic physics treats nucleus plus electrons; nuclear physics studies reactions and properties of the nuclei themselves.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: A gas contains a huge number of atoms.
Atoms in a gas rarely interact compared with the speed of atomic processes.
So atomic physics cannot say anything about gases.
Therefore treating each atom alone is a fair model.
beats.explain: Because atoms are alone nearly all the time, atomic physics does give the underlying theory for gases and plasmas.
